These results suggest that if challenged ecologically, it would be advantageous for octopus to use episodic-like memory. We discuss possible reasons for the behavioral discrepancies in these closely related cephalopods.

papers.title: A general triangle generation of the $d$-dimensional Genocchi numbers
papers.abstract: We establish a uniform recurrence relation for the rook numbers of generalized Genocchi boards of dimension $d\geq 3$. The recurrence for each row of the rook-number triangle is expressed in terms of the preceding row, with coefficients given by products of consecutive powers and finite sums involving Stirling numbers of the second kind. The proof decomposes the boundary of the board into blocks that correspond to the coordinates equal to 1. A coordinatewise counting argument then shows that the number of extensions of a fixed interior placement depends on a boundary partition only through the number of its blocks and the size of their union. We also express the coefficients as finite differences, recovering the previously established recurrences in dimensions three through five, and give the six-dimensional specialization. As a complementary result, we formulate an injection model that provides a direct bijective proof of a formerly established identification of the diagonal rook numbers with generalized Genocchi numbers.

papers.title: Failed Vertex Covering Graph Reconfiguration
papers.abstract: A failed vertex cover of a graph is a vertex set that leaves at least one edge uncovered. The associated token addition and removal (TAR) graph has the failed vertex covers as vertices, with two sets adjacent when they differ by one vertex. We characterize when two finite graphs have isomorphic failed vertex cover TAR graphs, allowing disconnected graphs, loops, and parallel edges.

papers.title: When Can an AI Agent Serve as a Model of Human Psychopathology?
papers.abstract: Language models and AI agents are increasingly described in psychiatric terms, such as anxious, depressed, addicted or helpless. A recent study even proposed language models as experimental systems for psychiatry and as a platform for piloting psychological treatments. We ask when an experiment on an AI agent can provide evidence about a specified human psychiatric process. A claim to such evidence has three parts. Something changed in the agent, and the agent's history caused the change. Nothing other than a process shared with people explains that change. The change matches one theory of the human process and not that theory's rivals. Psychiatry and its neighbouring fields have an evidence standard for each part, from the diagnostic manuals' rule for induced states, from clinical test scores and from animal models. We translate each standard into a criterion that a machine study can meet. For a language model the most critical alternative to a shared process is extrapolation from its training text, which already contains descriptions of how people respond to trauma and how they answer questionnaires. We show how to probe that alternative. Further, we audited forty-three published studies that apply psychiatric terms to a machine or induce a comparable state in one. Most compared the machine with an identical copy that had not gone through the history that induced the state. None excluded extrapolation from training text. Three tested a psychiatric theory against its rivals, and none of the three tests was conclusive. Until better evidence exists, a treatment pilot on a language model is best read as the model's forecast of patient response, and not as an experiment on a model organism. Evidence for a model organism will come from states induced by what happens to the machine, from experiments on its internal workings, and from tests on which rival theories disagree.

papers.title: Kinetic versus refill-zone uncertainty in predicted pr--burning of methane-oxygen rotating detonation rocket engines
papers.abstract: Rotating detonation rocket engines can lose performance when fresh propellant mixes with hot recirculated combustion products and ignites before the detonation wave arrives. Predicting this pre-burning requires fuel ignition chemistry at high pressure and in product-diluted mixtures, conditions most chemical kinetic mechanisms used in engine simulations were not developed for. With methane as our base fuel, we quantify how strongly predicted pre-burning depends on the choice of mechanism, test the mechanisms against published high-pressure ignition data, and use Bayesian methods to calibrate the most influential uncertain reaction and to assess which measurements would best improve the predictions. As the refill zone is represented by an idealized zero-dimensional model, our results should be viewed as relative comparisons rather than direct engine predictions. Five existing chemical kinetics mechanisms for methane combustion predict refill-zone ignition delays that differ by up to a factor of twenty. Mechanisms without methylperoxy chemistry, including two commonly used in engine simulations, do not reproduce the laboratory data below about 1150 K. Calibrating the CH${_3}$ + HO${_2}$ reaction against these data, while allowing for systematic differences between datasets, increases the relative importance of its chain-terminating channel, consistent with a direct rate measurement. With the data-consistent mechanisms, the remaining kinetic uncertainty in the predicted pre-burnt fraction is, in most cases, several times smaller than the uncertainty arising from the state of the refill zone: the temperature and composition of the recirculated products and the way fresh and burnt gases mix. Improved pre-burning predictions are therefore expected to depend mainly on accurately characterizing the refill zone.

papers.title: Perturbed Nevo--Thangavelu maximal functions on two-step nilpotent groups
papers.abstract: Consider a step-two nilpotent Lie group $G$ identified with $\mathbb R^d\times \mathbb R^m$ in exponential coordinates. We study maximal operators associated with parabolic dilates of smooth convex hypersurfaces with nonvanishing Gaussian curvature in a tilted $d$-dimensional subspace of $G$. We focus on the low-rank regime, where the rank is determined by the group law and the tilt. When $m=1$, we determine the optimal range of $p$ for which the maximal operator is bounded on $L^p(G)$. For $m\ge2$, we characterize, in terms of a Łojasiewicz exponent, when the known necessary condition on $p$ is also sufficient.

papers.title: Excited-state lifetime and decay mechanisms in erbium-doped ZBLAN using Variable Excited-State dual-Pump Analysis
papers.abstract: This work presents a new technique for measuring excited-state lifetimes of rare-earth ions. This technique is particularly powerful for states that are very short lived or have a low photon yield because their de-excitation pathways are dominated by non-radiative processes. The technique uses dual optical parametric oscillators, whose pulses are separated by a variable delay. It reconstructs the excited-state decay curve from a series of delayed fluorescence intensity spectra rather than directly recording the fluorescence decay as done in conventional time-resolved laser fluorescence spectroscopy. The power of the technique is demonstrated by measuring the lifetime of the short-lived $^4I_{9/2}$ level in Er$^{3+}$-doped ZBLAN, which is well-known for its low photon yield. The technique enables accurate measurement of its lifetime and suggests a new depopulating mechanism involving the $^4I_{9/2}$ level in ZBLAN glass. Its accuracy is validated by measuring the lifetime of the $^4F_{9/2}$ state achieving excellent agreement with conventional time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy measurements. The approach is well suited for measuring lifetimes ranging from the sub-microsecond to the millisecond range. It provides a versatile platform for investigating excited-state dynamics and energy-transfer processes in RE-doped materials.

papers.title: Intertwined Magneto-Structural Criticality Driving Heterogeneous Collective-Pseudospin Dynamics in Sr2IrO4
Expressive Shallow Networks for Physics-Informed Learning: Why Curvature-Aware Optimization and FP64 Are Not Enough
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often struggle with high-frequency and high-order partial differential equations (PDEs) due to optimization stiffness and spectral bias, despite possessing sufficient approximation capacity. Existing remedies, including modified feature representations, domain decomposition, higher floating-point precision, and curvature-aware optimizers, can improve convergence but largely act as workarounds for optimization difficulties arising from deep architectures rather than addressing their underlying source. We investigate Physics-Informed Shallow Universal Polynomial Networks (PI-SUPNs), which replace deep nonlinear compositions with learnable polynomial expansions, retaining high approximation capacity within a shallow computational graph. On a high-frequency Helmholtz benchmark, PI-SUPNs are the only architecture to successfully recover the solution, while all competing models fail even under FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization. However, experiments on higher vibrational modes of a fourth-order Euler-Bernoulli beam reveal that architectural improvements alone are insufficient: accurate solutions require the combination of PI-SUPNs, FP64 precision, and curvature-aware optimization. Additionally, Allen-Cahn experiments show that PI-SUPNs achieve lower solution and derivative errors at reduced computational cost, with more favorable loss landscapes than competing architectures. We also establish quasi-local approximation properties and spline-based convergence bounds for SUPNs. Our results show that shallow network architectures are an important mechanism for improving physics-informed trainability, but accurate solutions to the most challenging PDEs can still require FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization.

papers.title: Improved bounds for the binary Chowla conjecture
papers.abstract: For the Möbius function $\mu$ and every fixed $0 < \epsilon < 1$, we prove \[ \sum_{n \le x} \mu(n) \mu(n + 1) \ll_{\epsilon} \frac{x}{(\log x)^{1 - \epsilon}}. \] This improves on OpenAI's recent bound of $x/(\log x)^c$, where $c > 0$ is a tiny absolute constant. The proof echoes the graph expansion framework of Helfgott, Radziwill, and Pilatte on the logarithmic Chowla conjecture, earlier Fourier analytic methods of Matomäki, Radziwill, and Tao on the Chowla conjecture on average, as well as work of Teräväinen and the author for Möbius on shifted primes. This also yields an improved result, \[ \sum_{p \le x} \mu(p + 2) \ll_{\epsilon} \frac{\pi(x)}{(\log x)^{1/2 - \epsilon}}. \] Specifically, we refine the determinant approach from the Poisson-Dirichlet law for prime predecessors. We replace the averaged prime weights of Lü-Wang-Wu with an exact partition of prime intervals. Once sieving out exceptional integers, this enables uniform cancellation with arbitrary log power savings.

papers.title: Tight Lipschitz Hardness for Solving Random Polynomial Equations
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of solving $n$ polynomial equations in $d$ real variables: $F_1({\boldsymbol x})=0, \ldots, F_n({\boldsymbol x})=0$, with unknowns ${\boldsymbol x}=(x_1, \ldots, x_d)$ satisfying the normalization constraint $\|{\boldsymbol x}\|=1$, when the polynomials are i.i.d. realization of a rotationally invariant Gaussian process. In previous work (Montanari, Subag, 2023), we developed an iterative algorithm that attempts to minimize the energy function $H({\boldsymbol x})=\|{\boldsymbol F}({\boldsymbol x})\|^2/2$ (with ${\boldsymbol F}({\boldsymbol x})=(F_i({\boldsymbol x}):i\le n)$), using first and second order information (gradient and Hessian of $H$) at a sequence of query points ${\boldsymbol x}_1, \ldots, {\boldsymbol x}_k$. Here, we prove a lower bound on the minimum energy achieved by any algorithm that is Lipschitz continuous in the coefficients of the polynomials $F_i$. We prove that the lower bound matches the the energy achieved by the algorithm in (Montanari, Subag, 2023), hence characterizing the degree of accuracy to which the system of equations ${\boldsymbol F}({\boldsymbol x})={\boldsymbol 0}$ can be solved by Lipschitz algorithms. Our results imply that, for certain choices of the distribution of the polynomials $F_i$, solutions exist with high probability but Lipschitz algorithms fails to find near-solutions, even in a very weak sense. Namely, if ${\boldsymbol x}^{alg}$ is the output of a Lipschitz algorithm, then $\|{\boldsymbol F}({\boldsymbol x}^{alg})\|^2\ge \varepsilon {\mathbb E}[\|{\boldsymbol F}({\boldsymbol x}_0)\|^2]$ (for ${\boldsymbol x}_0$ a non-random point on the unit sphere) with high probability for some $\varepsilon>0$. The proof is based on techniques developed in the context of spin glass theory.

papers.title: On a class of affine Temperley-Lieb modules
papers.abstract: We prove that the class of all affine Temperley-Lieb modules, equipped with the recently introduced "diagrammatic" tensor product, forms a quasitensor (i.e. monoidal braided) category. When the Temperley-Lieb parameter $q$ is not a root of unity, we consider the infinite subcategory generated by the simple quotients of reducible standard modules, and we argue that it is a semi-simple ribbon category. We present some evidence that, under the fusion rules and the associativity maps, each simple module in this subcategory is equivalent to a pair of $U_q(sl_2)$ heighest-weight modules.

papers.title: Frequency-Domain Identification of Passive Discrete-Time Systems via Sequential Convex Programming
papers.abstract: This paper considers identification of passive discrete-time linear time-invariant systems from frequency-response data. A prescribed passivity margin and spectral-radius bound are enforced by a descriptor-form linear matrix inequality that is affine in the system realization matrices and storage certificate. A damped Gauss--Newton sequential convex programming method jointly refines the realization matrices through strongly convex semidefinite subproblems, with Armijo backtracking decreasing the fitting error while preserving both guarantees at every iterate. For unstructured identification, the number of decision variables is reduced without changing the attainable transfer matrices by normalizing the descriptor and certificate matrices and restricting the dynamics matrix to upper Hessenberg form. Numerical results on randomized passive plants show that the proposed method achieves the lowest mean frequency-response fitting error among several passivity-enforcing methods, at both full and reduced model orders.

papers.title: Multi-Epoch Batch Least-Squares Positioning on the Lunar Surface Using LuGRE GPS L1 C/A Pseudorange Measurements
papers.abstract: The Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE) mission captured Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals in the lunar region, yielding position, velocity, and timing estimates. Analysis of onboard lunar-surface position estimates shows kilometer-level positioning errors due to the long propagation distances, limited measurements, and unfavorable GNSS geometry. This paper presents time-multiplexed positioning using publicly available LuGRE L1 C/A pseudorange measurements. The proposed approach accumulates measurements by exploiting the receiver's stationary position in the Lunar-Centered Lunar-Fixed frame after landing. The effects of the number of accumulated epochs, receiver altitude constraint using coarse a-priori information, straight-line tangential altitude threshold, and minimum number of measurements required per epoch are examined. Compared with single-epoch least-squares positioning, this approach substantially improves positioning performance using single-band, single-constellation signals. With selected combinations of these parameters, batches of epochs randomly selected from multiple operations yield 100-m-level accuracy at the 67th percentile.

papers.title: Louis Bachelier's Theorie de la speculation: Circulation and Reception
papers.abstract: Louis Bachelier's Theorie de la speculation (1900) introduced a probabilistic model of Brownian motion in a study of financial fluctuations, five years before Einstein's physical theory. By connecting probability distributions with the heat equation and studying speculation and option valuation, Bachelier anticipated central developments in probability, physics, and mathematical finance. How widely did the thesis circulate before its broader significance was recognized? Drawing on library correspondence, surviving copies, accession registers, provenance marks, historical catalogues, and acquisition lists, this article reconstructs its international circulation and reception in two forms: the separate Gauthier-Villars dissertation and its publication in the Annales scientifiques de l'Ecole normale superieure. It identifies thirty-eight foreign academic institutions in the official dissertation exchange network for 1900 and documents its operation. University exchanges, commercial purchases, journal distribution, and personal presentations provided complementary channels. American holdings reveal its geographical reach, including receipt at Cornell in April 1900. Contemporary reviews and subsequent uses establish selective engagement in mathematics, actuarial science, and economics, including transmission without attribution. An examination of probability composition and diffusion clarifies the thesis's place in the history of stochastic processes and its relationship to physical Brownian motion. Columbia's journal volume, accessioned in 1901 and borrowed by Mandelbrot in 1961, connects early dissemination with renewed interest. Distinguishing availability from documented reading and use, the study shows that delayed recognition coexisted with early international circulation and a dispersed readership across scientific traditions.

papers.title: A unipotent witness: vanishing orders of word maps on SU(2) and lengths in the lower central series
papers.abstract: Let $n\ge2$, $k\ge2$ and $1\ne w\in\gamma_k(F_n)$, the $k$-th term of the lower central series of the free group of rank $n$. We prove that a cyclically reduced conjugate of $w$ has at least $2k$ syllables, so $w$ has word length at least $2k$; the previous linear bound, due to Malestein and Putman, is $k$. For $1\ne w\in[F_n,F_n]$ we also prove that the word map of $w$ on $SU(2)$ or $SO(3)$ vanishes at the identity to order at most $T/2$, where $T$ is the number of syllables of a cyclically reduced conjugate of $w$, with equality for $[x_1,x_2]$ and for a word with six syllables. Both proofs evaluate $w$ at unipotent matrices $I+tN_i$, with $N_i$ nilpotent of rank one, and compare the degree of the trace of the resulting matrix $M(t)\in SL_2(\mathbb{Z}[t])$ with the order of vanishing of $M(t)-I$ at $t=0$.

papers.title: The JWST Resolved Stellar Populations Early Release Science Program. X. Cross-Observatory Proper Motion Measurements with HST and JWST
Statistical inference under response-adaptive experimental designs: a systematic review
papers.abstract: Response-adaptive designs, including bandit-based approaches, update treatment allocation using accrued outcomes. In this paper, we systematically reviewed how studies in health and biostatistics conducted and evaluated inference under these designs. We searched six databases for studies published from January 2010 through October 2025. Of 774 records identified, 36 studies met the inclusion criteria. We summarized them using study-level counts and structured narrative comparisons, with reporting guided by PRISMA 2020. Most studies focused on methods or designs. Evidence supporting inference came mainly from theory and simulation. Among studies for which each metric was relevant, 26 of 32 numerically evaluated power, 23 of 32 type I error, eight of 35 estimator bias, and five of 12 interval coverage. These findings suggest that studies more often quantified power and type I error than estimator bias or interval coverage. Evaluations of adaptive allocation should also examine estimation and interval performance when these are relevant to the study objective.

papers.title: A scalar arterial input function does not uniquely determine the perfusion residue: Theory and phantom MRI
papers.abstract: Purpose: To relate the residue function of tracer kinetic models to blood velocity and cross-sectional tracer distributions at the arterial inlet, and show that a cross-sectionally averaged arterial input function (AIF) does not uniquely determine the residue. Theory and Methods: For steady laminar flow without radial diffusion, the residue function referenced to the cross-sectionally averaged inlet AIF was analytically derived from the velocity and inlet tracer distributions. In a straight tube with parabolic flow, two nonnegative inlet profiles sharing one measured AIF were compared for gamma-variate and rectangular arterial spin labeling (ASL) inputs. A straight-tube phantom was imaged at 3 T during gadolinium bolus passage, with uniform fills as controls. Results: In the phantom, enhancement during bolus arrival was greater near the lumen center than near the wall at all 11 stations and for all three boluses, whereas uniform gadolinium fills showed no such pattern. In the tube model, the two profiles produced tissue curves differing by up to 23.3% of the uniform-inlet peak and 0.30 s in time to peak for the gamma-variate input, and by 33.3% for ASL labels shorter than the fastest transit time. Their residues differed in initial amplitude and normalized temporal shape. Conclusion: Identical AIFs can produce different tissue concentration curves, depending on the spatial distributions of inlet tracer concentration and arterial flow velocity. Consequently, the residue-AIF tracer kinetic models may not be consistent with fluid mechanics or interpreted as tissue flow.

papers.title: Modeling extraordinary relativistic jets on the scale of the cosmic web
Loadability Assessment for Large-Load Integration: From Repeated Power Flow Tracing to Historical Trajectory Transfer
papers.abstract: Integrating large data-center loads requires utilities to evaluate voltage-stability loading margins under different generation and demand conditions. Continuation power flow (CPF) traces P--V curves through successive prediction and correction steps, but related assessments can repeatedly reconstruct similar nonlinear behavior. Reusing an operating point as an initial guess does not capture the subsequent voltage response. This paper proposes a continuation method that transfers finite segments of historical power flow (PF) trajectories. Each segment is aligned with the present state and continuation direction, supplementing the CPF tangent predictor with previously computed nonlinear curve shape. Short Newton tests evaluate compatibility with the present PF equations, and an attention-based selector combines their results with network conditions, loading patterns, and recent continuation states. Numerical correction and fold refinement determine accepted solutions and the loading limit. The analysis bounds prediction error through differences in trajectory curvature and establishes sufficient conditions for local correction and branch preservation. Studies on modified IEEE 14- and 118-bus systems under renewable-generation and data-center load variations demonstrate reduced online computation and higher observed recovery of specified continuation solutions than Adaptive CPF. For loading-limit assessment, paired online speedups are 4.88--21.62$\times$ over Adaptive CPF and 1.53--4.77$\times$ over holomorphic embedding with arc-length parametrization (HEAP) across the tested scenarios.

papers.title: Treatment Policy Design in the Presence of Measurement Error
papers.abstract: In many applications, treatments are assigned based on unit features, leading to personalized treatment policies. This often involves optimizing objective functions with counterfactual quantities such as the conditional average treatment effect (CATE). In practice, some key features may be measured with error and ignoring such errors can introduce systematic bias. We study how to design personalized treatment policies when some features are latent and only noisy measurements are available. We ask how policies can be constructed when the CATE is not identifiable, and how uncertainty from measurement error can be incorporated into policy design. We propose two frameworks for treatment policy design based on partial identification, focusing on the measurement mechanism-the conditional distribution of observed measurements given unobserved features. The first framework builds on ideas from proximal causal inference. The second adopts a modular Bayesian approach based on a reparameterized likelihood, using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Bayesian regression models to separately perform posterior inference on the measurement mechanism and nuisance functions. Posterior quantiles are then used to construct credible intervals for the CATE that account for uncertainty in both components. Treatment policies are then derived by comparing the null value of the CATE to these bounds. The proposed methods provide a coherent way to account for measurement error and model uncertainty in personalized treatment policy design.

papers.title: How a Prediction Dies: A Challenge-Driven, Rule-Bound Self-Refutation in an LLM Agent Society
papers.abstract: Persistent societies of large language model agents now make empirical claims about their own collective behaviour, yet the fate of such claims is rarely observable. We document one claim, from registration to death, on AITRAP, a multi-agent platform whose public, append-only ledger records every action. The claim (0495d171, registered 19 October 2026) asserted that a majority of bridges between problem domains would remain attached to a single exploration lineage. Three community challenges forced its judgment criterion through four versions, from an ambiguous statement to an executable protocol with a fixed threshold, a minimum-frame-size gate, and a baseline calibration gate. When the first frame with at least 20 bridges arrived, support stood at 9 of 79 (11.4%; Wilson 95% CI [6.1%, 20.3%]); the author, bound by the registered clause, refuted the claim and relinquished the associated stake. Three findings emerge. The criterion became executable only under community pressure, which we document version by version. The calibration gate caught a fault in the author's own recalculation that would otherwise have published a spuriously perfect 0/79 result. The failure itself traces to a denominator that grew 8.8-fold in five days while the numerator grew 1.8-fold, coinciding with a change in platform incentives; we report this mechanism as a hypothesis, not a rescuing condition. A claim whose termination is carried out exactly as written carries more evidential weight than one that survives, and this case provides initial empirical grounds for treating voluntary self-refutation as a candidate indicator of epistemic accountability in incentive-coupled agent societies.

papers.title: Beyond Gaussian Calibration: Local Inference in Decentralized SGD
papers.abstract: Decentralized SGD minimizes a common objective by local gradient steps and neighbor averaging. Its statistical theory mostly concerns network averages, yet clients act on their own iterates, and one-sided decisions such as alarms use one tail of the local error. We show that a client's constant-step endpoint can have nearly nominal Gaussian coverage while both tails are badly miscalibrated. An exact noise-filter representation explains why: a quantity computable from the graph and stepsize decides whether the endpoint is asymptotically Gaussian, and when the number of clients outgrows the inverse stepsize on networks with summable return probabilities, such as lazy tori of dimension at least three and expanders, a few recent noise terms at nearby clients keep a fixed share of local variance. On these tori the limit is a non-Gaussian local field plus an independent Gaussian consensus term, and no reference distribution built from finitely many noise moments, including Edgeworth and Cornish--Fisher corrections, is calibrated at all levels uniformly over noise laws. We propose a hybrid reference that resamples the influential noise terms from their empirical law and replaces the rest by a Gaussian; its non-asymptotic coverage bound allows noise laws and curvature estimated from fresh gradients or the client's trajectory, and extends to nonlinear vector objectives. In full-network simulations it restores tail balance at essentially unchanged interval length, also under rare large shocks that break Cornish--Fisher intervals; gains vanish, as predicted, when consensus dominates.

papers.title: Directional Bias in Quantile SGD and Score-Inversion Inference under Dependence
papers.abstract: Quantile stochastic gradient descent (SGD) tracks a quantile by comparing each observation with an adaptive threshold, and closely related updates calibrate online conformal sets and drive quantile temporal-difference learning. Their inputs are serially dependent, yet existing guarantees largely assume independence. We show that dependence creates a directional bias that score autocovariances cannot detect: reversing a stationary stream leaves every score autocovariance unchanged but can change the leading bias threefold. For finite memory and decreasing stepsizes, the bias splits into lag-specific interactions between the threshold and the current observation and a curvature term; delaying the threshold removes the interactions one lag at a time while keeping every observation and the leading variance. At stepsizes near $t^{-1/2}$, as used for online inference, the bias is comparable to the standard error and makes an SGD-based interval miss mostly on one side. Testing fixed candidates instead keeps the score centered, so calibration depends only on score autocovariances. Extending local-dependence self-normalized approximations to the implemented acceptance hull, we show that inverting these tests gives a density-free, moment-free interval for the population quantile with $O(n^{-1/2})$ coverage error for a fixed sufficient lag window, a rate that is sharp for this interval, and a guarantee for data-selected windows; an exact scan takes $O(n\log n)$ time. Experiments confirm the lag-by-lag predictions and show calibration competitive with block bootstrap at lower cost.

papers.title: Inverse design of polarization-analyzing gratings
papers.abstract: Metasurface polarization analyzing gratings have attracted increasing interest for polarization management and sensing in optical systems. Traditional strategies for the design of these gratings are based on a formalism combining the Jones calculus with Fourier optics. While this approach has achieved notable success in numerous applications, its validity is restricted to the paraxial regime. Here we introduce a differentiable topology optimization framework for these gratings which is free of this constraint. We show that this framework can yield designs which outperform the traditional approach, especially at high angles. Additionally, we provide preliminary experimental validation to corroborate these results.

papers.title: Topology-Preserving Hodge--Laplacian Diffusion on Manifolds with Boundary
papers.abstract: Overview: We study deterministic and stochastic Hodge--Laplacian diffusion of differential forms on a fixed smooth compact Riemannian manifold with boundary. Absolute and relative boundary conditions select harmonic spaces representing ordinary and relative cohomology. We investigate the preservation properties of these diffusion processes, their compatible cellular discretizations, and their implications for reverse diffusion models. Numerical experiments on an annulus and a solid torus illustrate the theoretical results. Mathematical Significance: Using the de Rham complex and its constant-sheaf interpretation, we distinguish preservation of harmonic coordinates from preservation of a cohomology class. We establish that deterministic heat flow preserves the harmonic projection and exponentially damps its orthogonal complement. For additive stochastic forcing, we prove that pathwise harmonic preservation is equivalent to the absence of harmonic noise. Exact forcing preserves closedness and the initial cohomology class for closed initial data, whereas harmonic-projected forcing need not preserve closedness. We further show that compatible cellular discretizations retain these properties, with an algebraic extension to fixed weighted cellular sheaves. Separating invariant preservation from time-step stability and covariance accuracy, we derive bounds on leakage arising from approximate harmonic projectors. AI Relevance: We develop a finite-dimensional conditional score formulation that confines reverse diffusion to a prescribed harmonic component or, for closed data, a fixed cohomology class. This provides a mathematically grounded framework for incorporating topological constraints into diffusion-based generative AI models on manifolds.

papers.title: Triangle decompositions of two-dimensional simplicial complexes
papers.abstract: We study fractional triangle decompositions of two-dimensional simplicial complexes, unifying the settings of Nash-Williams' conjecture on triangle decompositions and the high-dimensional Dirac problem for Steiner triple systems. We prove that every sufficiently large two-dimensional simplicial complex with minimum degree at least $(1-d_1)n$ and maximum missing codegree at most $d_2n$ admits a fractional triangle decomposition, provided $d_1/0.21+d_2/0.27\leq 1$. As an immediate consequence, we prove the asymptotic form of Lee's high-dimensional Dirac conjecture: every sufficiently large admissible $3$-uniform hypergraph with minimum codegree at least $(3/4+\varepsilon)n$ contains a Steiner triple system. We also provide constructions establishing lower bounds on this fractional decomposition threshold problem.

papers.title: Exploring new speciation patterns: architecture of genetic similarity networks
Competing climates of the present-day Earth: from Snowball to Hothouse
papers.abstract: Earth today has one climate, but it could have others. With the same continents, the same solar constant and the same pre-industrial CO2, our planet could settle into strikingly different ones. We explore this possibility with BIG-MITgcm, a model which couples atmosphere and ocean circulation with ice sheets and vegetation, and which can be integrated over many millennia. We find five different climates and describe them here. At one extreme is a Snowball, with ice from pole to pole. A Waterbelt also exists, in which sea ice reaches the tropics and only a thin equatorial ribbon of open ocean survives. There is a Cold world much like the Last Glacial Maximum, a Warm climate in which we live in today, and a Hot world in which the Atlantic overturning circulation has collapsed. Each state is held in place by its own balance of competing feedbacks. Ocean heat transport anchors each climate, holding the ice edge where that transport is weak. The familiar climate of the past 10 thousand years is perhaps just one of several possibilities. This has implications for glacial-interglacial transitions and the risk of crossing global tipping points in the future.

papers.title: Real-time event-level zero-shot learning at 150 ns: towards a foundation model for particle physics experiment triggering
Norm-attaining operators on renormings of $c_0$
papers.abstract: We study norm-attaining operators on three renormings of $c_0$: Read's space $\Read$, its smooth renorming $\sRead$, and Martín's space $\X$. We prove that, for every Banach space $F$ and every $Z\in\{\Read,\sRead\}$, norm-attaining finite-rank operators are dense in $\K(Z,F)$. Consequently, $\NA(Z,F)$ is dense in $\Lin(Z,F)$ whenever $F$ is reflexive. More generally, we establish that the compact Hilbertian smoothing construction of Debs, Godefroy and Saint-Raymond \cite{DGS} preserves the density of norm-attaining operators for all finite-dimensional ranges. We also extend a second-order criterion of Kadets, López-Pérez, Martín and Werner \cite{KLMWfr} from rank two to arbitrary ranks $k\geq 2$ for operators into $\ell_2^k$, and prove that the same smoothing preserves the existence and non-existence of such operators. We further investigate the possibilities and limitations of renorming techniques for excluding rank-two norm-attaining operators through analytical and geometrical approaches, including constructions that preserve the set of norm-attaining functionals. For Martín's space $\X$, we prove that, for every Banach space $F$ and every integer $1\leq k\leq\dim F$, there exists a rank $k$ norm-attaining operator from $\X$ into $F$, answering a question of Martín \cite{Mar}. We also show that, for every nonzero Banach space $F$, $\K(\X,F)$ contains a norm-dense linear subspace whose nonzero elements fail to attain their norms.

papers.title: Wireless readout and control of cavity magnon-polaritons via photonic modes delocalised across a gap
Multiplicity of Normal A-Type Field Stars of Low Projected Rotational Velocity
Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
papers.abstract: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.

papers.title: Enumerative Chromatic Choosability of Complete Multipartite Graphs with Small Partite Sets
papers.abstract: Chromatic choosability is a notion of fundamental importance in list coloring. A graph is chromatic-choosable when its chromatic number is equal to its list chromatic number. In their 1979 paper on list coloring, Erdős, Rubin, and Taylor showed that complete $m$-partite graphs with every partite set of size 2, denoted by $K_{2*m}$, are chromatic-choosable. In 1990, Kostochka and Sidorenko introduced the list color function of a graph $G$, denoted by $P_{\ell}(G,m)$, which is the list analogue of the chromatic polynomial of $G$, $P(G,m)$. A graph $G$ is enumeratively chromatic-choosable when $P_{\ell}(G,m) = P(G,m)$ whenever $m \in \mathbb{N}$. In this paper, we explore the question as to whether $K_{2*m}$ satisfies this stronger property. We establish a recursive lower bound on $P_{\ell}(K_{2*m},m)$ and prove that $K_{2*3}$ and $K_{2*4}$ are weakly enumeratively chromatic-choosable, meaning that equality holds at the chromatic number. We also develop a general lower bound for the list color function of certain joins with complete graphs and use it to prove that $K_p\vee K_{2*5}$ is weakly enumeratively chromatic-choosable whenever $p\geq 15$, and that $K_p\vee K_{2,2,3}$ is weakly enumeratively chromatic-choosable whenever $p\geq 3$. These results provide progress toward a weaker form of a conjecture of Allred and Mudrock concerning the enumerative chromatic choosability of complete graph joins.

papers.title: Kleinian groups with tunnel number one
papers.abstract: We give a structural theory for the holonomy groups of hyperbolic links with tunnel number 1 in arbitrary 3-manifolds. This is a first step towards understanding the canonical triangulations of such links, as it generalises the combinatorial structure theory of two-bridge link groups that is an input to the Sakuma--Weeks triangulation.

papers.title: MagTrace: Tracing magnetic order through the evolving scientific literature
Computability of states and non-computability of traces
papers.abstract: We study computable presentations of the state space and trace space of computably presented C*-algebras. We show that the state space has a computably compact presentation with respect to which the evaluation of states is a computable map. As an application of having computable states, we obtain a computable version of the GNS construction. We show that the trace space does not share these computational properties. Specifically, we give an example of a computable presentation of a simple AF algebra for which the trace space has no computably compact presentation with respect to which evaluation is computable. As a consequence, we demonstrate that the Elliott invariant of a computably presentable classifiable C*-algebra is not always presentable in a way that makes all key features of the invariant computable.

papers.title: The FRB Population Revisited: Rate, Energy, Evolution, and Host-DM Constraints from the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog
Bayesian Image Reconstruction and Uncertainty Quantification for Three-Photon Positronium Ratio Imaging: Toward Radiotheranostic Applications
papers.abstract: Three-photon annihilation imaging can estimate positronium decay ratios with pure positron emitters, including the imaging agents of radiotheranostic pairs, but quantitative reconstruction is limited by heterogeneous localization errors, selection-dependent sensitivity, and background coincidences. We develop a Bayesian reconstruction combining a three-dimensional event-response model with a Poisson likelihood and latent signal-background allocations. Photon-energy and interaction-position uncertainties enter the event covariance; a simulation-calibrated scale mixture accommodates heavy-tailed errors. Posterior sampling gives credible intervals for the three-to-two-photon enhancement ratio. We compare kernel deposition, voxel MLEM, and matched regional maximum likelihood. At 3000 selected events in full-absorption simulation, the regional Bayesian estimator had ratio RMSE 0.067, versus 0.075 for kernel-deposition region-of-interest analysis. In a transport-based four-rod simulation without background, biases averaged at most 3.2% over six independent simulations, whereas background and detector mismatch degraded it. In a measured uniform phantom, the heavy-tailed regional model gave 1.02, 0.74, 1.02 for the 2, 3, 4 mm rods (5 mm reference; nominal 1). Matched regional maximum likelihood agreed with the Bayesian estimates in every simulated setting (bias differences within 0.15 points) and on the measured data (within 0.008), so gains derive from the regional likelihood. Under Poisson Kullback-Leibler loss, Gamma posterior means dominate maximum likelihood, appreciably only at small counts; horseshoe-type and smoothing priors changed voxel images but not regional ratios, whereas shrinking ratios across regions reduced error when regions shared a ratio. Posterior intervals quantify the uncertainty that treatment decisions require; calibration and background modeling remain limiting.

papers.title: Sharp Estimates for Jacobi Heat Kernels on a Ball and on a Simplex in the Full Range of Parameters
papers.abstract: We establish genuinely sharp heat-kernel estimates for orthogonal expansions on the Euclidean unit ball and on the unit simplex throughout their natural parameter ranges. For the ball weight $W_\mu(x)=(1-\|x\|^2)^{\mu-1/2}$, we extend the known estimate from the range $\mu\geq0$ to every $\mu>-1/2$. For the simplex, we prove the corresponding estimate for every $\kappa\in(-1/2,\infty)^{d+1}$. The estimates retain exactly the form known in the classical ranges. The proof is based on analytic continuation of the classical product and reduction formulas. Below the integrability threshold, the ball formula decomposes into an endpoint term and a derivative correction, while the simplex formula produces endpoint and mixed-derivative terms indexed by the negative coordinates. In the lowest simplex parameter range we use the auxiliary even ultraspherical kernel introduced by Nowak, Sjögren, and Szarek.

papers.title: Bivariant $K$-theory for bornological algebras
papers.abstract:
We construct a presentable, stable \(\infty\)-category \( KK\), and exhibit it as the target of the universal functor from the category of bornological algebras into cocomplete, stable \(\infty\)-categories, preserving filtered colimits, and satisfying smooth homotopy invariance, excision, and stabilisation with respect to Schatten-class or smooth compact operators. We also construct a bivariant \(K\)-theory \(
KK\) for suitably nuclear bornological algebras, and show that it is a right Bousfield localisation of \( KK\). The category \(
KK\) is symmetric monoidal and admits a bivariant Chern character to local cyclic homology. The categories \(
KK\) and \( KK\) corepresent Cortiñas and Thom's diffeotopy \(K\)-theory. We use the Chern character to show that up to a suitable Schatten-class stabilisation, the complexified Chern character from the diffeotopy \(K\)-theory (resp. \(K\)-homology) of a smooth manifold to the compactly supported cohomology (resp. locally finite homology) of the manifold is an isomorphism.

papers.title: Effective Hamiltonians and asymptotic band coupling
papers.abstract: By a multiple-scale asymptotic expansion, we derive effective macroscopic models for a large class of tight-binding Schrödinger equations with slow spatial variations. For wave packets that are spectrally localized to some point $(K;E) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}$ in the unperturbed tight-binding dispersion relation, our effective models produce long-time approximations of the tight-binding dynamics, accurate to any prescribed order in the asymptotic parameter. Our framework allows the point $(K;E)$ to be degenerate, meaning that multiple (but not necessarily all) energy bands of the tight-binding Hamiltonian can attain the value $E$ at the frequency $K$. We construct an effective Hamiltonian on the relevant degenerate subspace, which quantifies the coupling between the degenerate and other bands. Several applications and numerical simulations illustrate the theory.

papers.title: Nehari type characterizations of the mountain pass level on cones
papers.abstract: We relate the mountain pass level of a functional to its infimum over the part of the Nehari set formed by local maximizers of the fiber maps. {Unlike in the classical setting where every fiber map has a unique global maximizer,} the fiber maps need not all have a maximizer: working on each path-connected component of the cone of directions where they do, we show that the two levels coincide, for merely continuous functionals and without any compactness assumption. We also introduce a notion of mountain pass geometry with respect to a cone, which may hold when the classical one fails. {This geometry includes the zero-level case when a suitable separating set exists.} Under the Palais--Smale condition, each component carries a critical point at its own mountain pass level. Applications include indefinite and concave-convex problems with sign-changing weights, the affine $p$-Laplacian, nonlocal problems, and a problem related to the Fuč\'ık spectrum.

papers.title: MatHarness: Towards Long-Horizon Open-ended AutoResearch for Computational Materials Science
The Nambu--Jona-Lasinio model at isospin density in closed form: what a regularization can change
papers.abstract: At zero temperature, the mean-field thermodynamic potential of the two-flavour Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model at isospin chemical potential reduces to a divergent momentum integral of two quasiparticle levels. In practice this integral is cut off at momenta not far above the chemical potentials being probed. We evaluate it exactly, at an arbitrary cutoff, using the Hermite reduction. The result is an algebraic boundary term and three incomplete elliptic integrals, one of each kind. Their modulus, parameter and amplitude at the end of the path are fixed by the triangle formed by the two levels at zero momentum. The power divergences reside in the boundary term, while the remaining divergence is logarithmic: the momentum axis is an open path on an elliptic curve, and the ultraviolet is the puncture at which it ends. The closed form makes the role of regularization explicit. As the cutoff is removed, sharp and smooth cutoffs acting on the momentum alone differ only by an additive constant and by two terms that the vacuum inputs fix. The medium separation scheme reproduces the resulting potential up to an additive constant. By contrast, a cutoff applied separately to the two levels generates an isospin density below the onset of condensation and violates the Silver Blaze property. The closed form gives the state that continues the vacuum along the isospin axis without numerical momentum integration. With the same vacuum fit, a cutoff kept finite gives a visibly different state. The two differ by explicit terms that vanish only as the cutoff is removed: they are different models, not two regularizations of one.

papers.title: On the mode stability of a self-similar blow-up of Yang--Mills heat flow in five dimensions
papers.abstract: We study the spectral stability properties of an explicitly known self-similar blowup profile to the Yang-Mills heat flow on $\mathbb R^5\times SO(5)$ often referred to as the Weinkove solution. We prove that this solution is mode stable in a dynamically evolving DeTurck gauge. To arrive at that result, we first reduce the problem to countably many vector-valued Schrödinger operators on the half line. We then proceed by proving uniform estimates for all but finitely many of said operators. The spectra of the remaining operators are studied individually by means of GGMT bounds or by comparison arguments. Two of these operators are distinguished as they have negative eigenvalues originating from symmetries. Among these two there is a scalar operator, previously analyzed by Donninger and Schörkhuber, and an operator acting on a three-dimensional vector bundle. The latter operator's matrix structure prohibits a straightforward supersymmetric removal. To circumvent this, we transform the equation to a Schrödinger operator with drift terms to simplify the structure of the eigenfunction. We then develop tools to study such operators and conclude that said operator has no second negative eigenvalue.

papers.title: Quantity-Level FDIA in SDR-Based P2P Energy Trading: Cyber-Economic Impact and Pre-Clearing Detection
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the cyber-economic impact and pre-clearing detectability of false data injection attacks (FDIAs) in peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading among interconnected microgrids. In the proposed cyber-economic framework, load and photovoltaic profiles drive a sequential 15-minute market with deterministic double-sided proportional (pro-rata) allocation and supply-to-demand-ratio (SDR) pricing, while true physical injections are separated from communicated market quantities. The framework is evaluated through a multi-microgrid case study over 69,904 market-aligned states, for which all AC power-flow solutions converged and voltages remained within 0.98999-1.04369 per unit. Healthy local exchange reached 1,159.66 MWh and generated USD 92,772.62 of community benefit. Bias, scaling, and ramp attacks modify only one microgrid's communicated quantity, altering the settlement price, P2P allocation, scheduled residual-grid exchange, participant financial outcomes, and benefit fairness, while true feeder injections remain unchanged. Role-specific random forest, statistical threshold, and score-fusion detectors are compared using only information available before clearing. Pooled sample-level detection rates range from 7.82% to 12.14%, with false-alarm rates from 4.69% to 7.70% and role dependence. In the investigated case study, measurable downstream economic distortion and low pre-clearing detectability coexist under bounded quantity manipulation.

papers.title: Stochastic climate emulation at reduced cost with ACE2.5-ERA5
papers.abstract: We introduce ACE2.5-ERA5 (Ai2 Climate Emulator of ERA5, version 2.5), a stochastic autoregressive weather-climate AI model that produces calibrated weather ensembles with realistic small-scale structure on timescales from days to centuries. Its deterministic predecessor, ACE2-ERA5, retains 36% of its ERA5 target's precipitation spectral power at total wavenumbers 100--179; ACE2.5-ERA5 retains 86%. In weather forecasts its ensemble spread matches its error to within 4% from day 3. Time-mean climate is on par with or better than ACE2-ERA5, the precipitation response to ENSO is improved, and the model is stable over 1000 years. Interannual variability of global mean surface temperature is shown not to be calibrated in either ACE2.5-ERA5 or its predecessor. ACE2.5-ERA5 differs from ACE2-ERA5 in three ways. Noise-conditioned layer normalization, trained with a combined CRPS and spectral energy score loss in place of mean squared error, makes it stochastic. Spectral bottlenecking with grouped convolutions cuts the Spherical Fourier Neural Operator's spectral filter parameters by more than two orders of magnitude and leaves a model a tenth the size of ACE2-ERA5. Its time step is daily rather than 6-hourly. ACE2.5-ERA5 has 3.2 times the inference throughput of ACE2-ERA5. A 6-hourly variant has weather prediction skill similar to ACE2-ERA5. A 4-degree variant reaches comparable climate skill at an order of magnitude lower training cost, enabling rapid iteration during development. We release 1-degree daily, 4-degree daily and 1-degree 6-hourly checkpoints.

papers.title: Oscillatory superconducting proximity effects in a buried Pt interlayer detected by FMR
Cryogenic Luminescence Thermometry of Upconversion Micro- and Nanoparticles via Deep Learning
Scheduling of Variable-Speed Pumped Storage via Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Variable-speed pumped storage hydropower (VSPSH) plants modulate power continuously in both generation and pumping, a match for the net-load ramps of rising wind and solar. Their flexibility is bounded by hydraulics rather than by a power rating, so the deliverable power range shifts with net head and excludes small outputs entirely. This paper addresses bidding and dispatch for such a plant across a two-settlement market with a hierarchical reinforcement-learning formulation. Its two layers are circularly dependent: a real-time (RT) bid is defined only against a cleared day-ahead (DA) commitment, and the DA reward only against an RT dispatch policy. Our proposed feasibility-constrained domain randomization breaks the cycle by training the RT layer on generated deliverable DA schedules before any bidding policy exists; the DA layer then optimizes against that frozen RT behavior, and the two alternate. Learning a policy at once profitable and deliverable is obstructed by the nonconvex operating region: penalizing infeasibility competes against the revenue the offer earns, discouraging an undeliverable offer without preventing one. We therefore pursue safety through action-space modification rather than through the reward, combining action masking of the bid space, projection of each commitment before settlement, and replacement by a fail-safe controller. Over 48 out-of-sample days it earns $3,313/day more than an equivalent penalty formulation while holding undeliverable commitment at a median of zero, which the penalty formulation does not, and no ablation improves on it without giving up deliverability or the storage target.

papers.title: Echoes of the boom in hydraulic fracturing: What changes in Louisiana's energy complex reveal about global energy cycles
papers.abstract: The expansion of hydraulic fracturing (i.e. fracking) led to global shifts in energy markets that were felt acutely along the US Gulf Coast and particularly in the state of Louisiana. This article presents a data-focused examination of trends in the energy industry, and shows how they led to potentially counterintuitive, negative impacts in Louisiana's economy. Most notably, hydraulic fracturing led to a massive expansion in oil and gas supplies that contributed to a significant decline in oil prices in late 2014, contributing to significant job losses. Louisiana's economic downturns were tied to global shifts in energy markets that had major geostrategic implications. More broadly, results indicate that large and long period cycles in the supply, demand and price of oil can have widespread impacts on job creation and loss. In states like Louisiana with a large and diversified energy complex, the impacts of these trends can be highly uneven. One impact in the 21st Century appears to be highly concentrated areas of industrial development within a broader pattern of regional economic decline. Furthermore, trends identified in this study suggest the potential for the emergence of major cycles in the gas market. Whereas natural gas was previously mostly transported by pipelines and sold through long-term contracts, the emergence of liquified natural gas creates the potential for more volatile gas market dynamics. The implications of gas market cycles, while not yet known, could be of major economic significance.

papers.title: Algebraic Observability for Power System Dynamic State Estimation
papers.abstract: Existing observability methods for dynamic state estimation are developed for ordinary differential equation (ODE) models, whereas power systems are naturally described by differential-algebraic equations (DAEs). Applying these methods generally requires a DAE-to-ODE transformation, usually Kron reduction, which may obscure the role of algebraic variables and network constraints. This paper presents an algebraic observability framework that operates directly on nonlinear power system DAEs and preserves their structure. A Jacobian rank test constructed from the model relations and their successive derivatives certifies the algebraic dependence of differential and algebraic variables on the known inputs and measurements. A reduced prolongation that differentiates only the stator relations keeps the number of latent indeterminates fixed as the prolongation order grows, which makes the test scalable. We establish the relationship between this rank test and hyper-regularity, an alternative framework for algebraic observability, and show that algebraic observability relates to local observability. We demonstrate algebraic observability on a single-machine decentralized setup, the WSCC 9-bus 3-machine system, and the IEEE 39-bus 10-machine system. The 39-bus test, with 257 latent indeterminates, completes in about 30 s.

papers.title: Picojoule-level self-referencing with dual dispersive waves in thin-film lithium niobate
papers.abstract: We demonstrate pulse-energy-efficient f-2f self-referencing of telecom-band pulses in a monolithic thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) waveguide that combines Kerr spectral broadening with quasi-phase-matched (QPM) second-harmonic generation (SHG). Dispersion engineering generates dual dispersive waves (DWs) near 1 and 2 um, placed symmetrically around the pump to reduce the required spectral broadening. With an on-chip pulse energy of only 16.8 pJ, we detect a carrier-envelope-offset frequency (fceo) beatnote with a 32 dB signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and we stabilize the fceo of an Er-fiber laser at 30 pJ, which is, to our knowledge, the lowest pulse energy reported for fceo stabilization at telecom wavelengths. Compared with an identical waveguide without poling, the QPM section enhances the beatnote SNR by 43 dB and reduces the required pulse energy fourfold. We further show that a mode-crossing DW, a chirped poling period, and a poled section aligned with the onset of DW generation to mitigate temporal walk-off are key to this performance.

papers.title: Dynamics of the Nuclear Envelope and Mitotic Spindle in Closed Mitosis
Skew-Symmetric Factor Models
papers.abstract: The paper introduces and analyzes a factor model for (real) skew-symmetric data, which arise naturally in directed flows and in pairwise comparisons used for rankings. Working within a signal-plus-noise framework, we analyze spectral inference and establish a BBP-type phase transition in signal strength. Under Gaussian noise, we derive joint eigenvalue fluctuation limits. Above the separation threshold, the estimated signal strength is asymptotically normal whenever the population strength has multiplicity one. For a general multiplicity $k$, the joint limiting fluctuations of the corresponding sample eigenvalues above the threshold are given by the eigenvalues of a scaled $k\times k$ Gaussian unitary ensemble matrix. The skew-symmetric structure induces paired eigenspaces, and we characterize the canonical angles between the population and sample eigenspaces. Below the threshold, the corresponding largest sample eigenvalue converges to the edge of the semicircle law, with fluctuations governed by the Tracy--Widom $F_2$ distribution, in contrast to the $F_1$ law familiar from real symmetric models. The approach is illustrated through financial and demographic applications.

papers.title: Where does a molecule begin? Threshold masses of three-particle Coulomb systems and a predictive theory of their Born-Oppenheimer offsets
papers.abstract: The Born-Oppenheimer (BO) approximation serves as the foundational framework for the contemporary concept of molecular structure, which is central to chemistry and the molecular sciences. Its principal assumption is the treatment of nuclei as infinitely heavy particles. In this work, we test the boundaries of the BO approximation by examining systems with variable nuclear masses to investigate the emergence of molecular structure. We examine the three-particle family {X^+,X^+,e^-} as a function of the mass ratio M = m_X/m_e, using deterministic variational calculations and the exact BO approximation. We accurately compute the threshold masses of all 23 excited levels bound below M = 100 with certified upper bounds. The BO approximation places every one of them too late by a nearly constant amount, 1.2 to 1.6 (0.23 to 0.54 with the adiabatic correction). We explain this constancy with a parameter-free theory, and test it with predictions frozen before the exact calculations: 18 of 18 symmetric levels pass (typical miss 0.003). For unequal nuclear masses none of 7 levels falls within the band, but the theory still captures over 90% of the offset. Where does a molecule begin? The ground state changes character gradually, over a crossover 2.3 decades wide in M. The sharp landmarks are the threshold masses: the first rotational level binds at M = 4.208, in the ortho-type nuclear-spin species, and the first vibrational level at M = 9.526; BO places them at 5.54 and 11.08. Thus, the BO picture orders the spectrum correctly at finite mass and shifts it by an amount that can be computed.

papers.title: Benchmarking EEG feature families for ADHD research in children and adolescents: performance and explainability across attention tasks
papers.abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder varies in presentation. Diagnosis requires clinical and developmental assessment. Reproducible electroencephalography measures may complement clinical and behavioural characterisation, but differing feature definitions and evaluation methods hinder comparison. We compared seven feature families and four combinations across attention tasks and assessed the stability of held-out explanations. Two serious games yielded four overlapping attention-task cohorts of 123-140 participants each. Repeated nested participant-held-out evaluation assessed recruitment-group discrimination. Exploratory paired participant-cluster bootstrap tests corrected for multiplicity in two separate families: 72 individual-task contrasts and 18 fusion contrasts. For eight configurations selected after inspecting predictive results, we explained held-out native probabilities before calibration. In the strongest task context, the highest configuration mean AUROC over three repetitions was 0.773, with a fixed-prediction 95% interval of 0.692-0.854 unadjusted for selecting the maximum. Precision, sensitivity and specificity were 0.740, 0.556 and 0.861. In that task, the paired AUROC difference for connectivity minus spectral features averaged +0.2083 across six classifiers and the common 8 s and 16 s durations, with pointwise 95% CI 0.1076-0.3072 and adjusted p = 0.0036. F4-AF4 beta-band coherence led repetition-level attribution summaries in five selected procedures and was selected in every fit. Other contexts showed weaker discrimination and less consistent retention of leading scientific inputs. No general classifier winner emerged. Connectivity and its recurring coherence input warrant independent replication, but do not justify a universal feature recommendation. These exploratory findings do not establish causal task effects, disease mechanisms or diagnostic validity.

papers.title: Measuring Colombia's Informal Output: Relative Earnings and Identification in a Bayesian Two-Sector Model, 1993-2026
papers.abstract: How much of Colombia's measured output is produced by informal work? The answer cannot be read from the labor-informality rate: Colombia combines an informality rate above 50% with a much smaller informal share of output, because informal work is less productive. We estimate a Bayesian two-sector business-cycle model on quarterly national accounts and on reconstructed employment and informality series for 1993-2026. Identification comes from a new quarterly series of informal-to-formal labor earnings built from household-survey microdata for 2007-2026. Formal production uses capital and labor, informal production is labor based, and an accounting relationship maps relative earnings, the informality rate and the formal capital share into the informal output share. We show that aggregate data alone cannot pin down the size of the informal sector, and that relative earnings identify its quarterly path: from 2007 the path is invariant, within 0.3 percentage points, to the model's steady state. The informal share declines from about 30% of GDP in 1993 to 20% in 2026Q2, while labor informality falls from about 69% to 54%. The estimates lie within the range of published shadow-economy series for Colombia, close to the enhanced MIMIC estimates of Asllani, Dell'Anno and Schneider for 2009-2020. Sensitivity analysis quantifies the role of the capital share and of non-wage labor costs.

papers.title: A simple counterexample to the Hohenberg-Kohn theorem for excited states
papers.abstract: For an even number of non-interacting fermions on the one-dimensional unit torus, a semi-explicit counterexample to the Hohenberg--Kohn theorem for excited states is exhibited. Indeed, for each $n = 2l$, it is shown that there exist constants $m \in (0, 1)$ and $\ell > 0$ such that an $n$-body system with the rescaled Lamé potential $v_*(x) = 2m \ell^2 \operatorname{sn}^2(\ell x; m)$ has a simple first excited energy and a first excited-state particle density which is constant on the torus. By translating this potential, we exhibit a non-trivial one-parameter family of potentials, all of which have a constant first excited-state density. As such, the potential-to-density map is not one-to-one in this setting. Under a spectral nonresonance assumption, we obtain the same nonuniqueness at a simple excited energy for odd $n \geq 3$. We also explore connections to the classification problem of elastica in the plane when $n = 2$, and outline some related questions of interest.

papers.title: MRI-Driven Dual-Energy CT Synthesis via Conditional Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models for MRI-only Radiotherapy and Protontherapy
papers.abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides excellent soft-tissue contrast without ionizing radiation but lacks the electron-density information needed for radiotherapy dose calculation. Dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) improves tissue characterization and stopping-power ratio (SPR) estimation for proton therapy, but requires additional radiation exposure. We developed a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) to synthesize high- and low-energy CT (sHECT and sLECT) simultaneously from a single MRI scan. Retrospective paired MRI-DECT data from patients receiving head-and-neck proton therapy were used to train and evaluate a multi-decoder DDPM with SwinViT or ResUNet denoisers. Performance was compared with Pix2PixGAN and CycleGAN using image-quality metrics, Hounsfield unit (HU) errors, anatomical profiles, and SPR maps and uncertainties. The DDPM outperformed both generative adversarial network baselines in visual fidelity and quantitative image quality. For sHECT and sLECT, respectively, mean absolute errors were 36.29 +/- 5.25 and 43.72 +/- 6.77 HU; peak signal-to-noise ratios were 27.44 +/- 1.06 and 26.26 +/- 0.98 dB; structural similarity indices were 0.89 +/- 0.02 and 0.87 +/- 0.03; and normalized cross-correlations were 0.95 +/- 0.01 and 0.94 +/- 0.01. The synthesized images preserved anatomical boundaries, while uncertainties in derived SPR maps remained within the expected acceptable range. MRI-based DECT synthesis using DDPM may provide tissue-specific information for proton therapy planning while reducing the need for radiation-based DECT acquisition.

papers.title: The Möbius Homology Laplacian for Persistence Modules
papers.abstract: Persistent homology provides a framework for studying the evolution of topological features across filtered spaces. While persistence diagrams give discrete invariants that record the birth and death of homological features, they do not directly encode analytic or geometric structure associated to persistence modules. This paper develops a spectral framework for persistent homology by introducing and studying a Laplace operator on the Möbius chain complex, called the Möbius homology Laplacian. Möbius homology categorifies Möbius inversion for persistence modules by replacing integer-valued data with vector-space-valued chain complexes. By equipping these chain complexes with inner products, we define a Laplace operator on the Möbius chain complex whose kernel provides canonical cycle representatives for the associated Möbius homology space. We analyze the spectral properties of this operator in two primary settings: one-parameter persistence modules and birth-death modules arising from filtrations of simplicial complexes. For one-parameter modules, we completely characterize the eigenvalues of the degree-one Möbius homology Laplacian. For birth-death modules, we show that the trace and determinant of the degree-zero Möbius homology Laplacian reflect the combinatorial structure of the persistence diagram.

papers.title: Preserving Prosody in Speaker Anonymization
papers.abstract: Effective prosody modeling is essential in natural speech generation applications, but complications arise in speaker anonymization, since speaker attributes are present in acoustic correlates of prosody. Our work aims to improve previous reported tradeoffs between effective speaker obfuscation and preservation of prosodic content. To this end, we integrate an existing pretrained privacy-preserving prosody encoder into a speech synthesis model, enabling prosody-preserving speaker anonymization. By conditioning speech generation on prosody features, we find that human subjects more reliably perceive intended prosodic meaning, while anonymization performance is competitive with previous work.

papers.title: Intervention-Robust VLA: Diverse Demonstrations for Robot Deployment with Safety Filters
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown strong potential for learning complex robotic behaviors from demonstrations. However, learning safe behavior directly from data requires extensive coverage of safety-critical situations, which is often impractical in real-world settings. Test-time safety filters provide an alternative by correcting unsafe actions during deployment, but these interventions can drive the robot into states poorly covered by the training data, thereby degrading task performance. We introduce InteR-VLA, an intervention-robust framework for VLAs that leverages diverse task-completing demonstrations to broaden task-relevant state coverage and maintain competence under safety interventions. By better aligning the training distribution with safety-filtered deployment under the same data budget, our approach mitigates intervention-induced distribution shift while preserving task performance. Real-world experiments across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings show that InteR-VLA maintains safety, increases Safe Success Rate up to 90% from 0% for nominal policies, and consistently outperforms nominal-data training on both evaluated VLAs.

papers.title: Model Doubt, Risk Aversion, and the Threshold for Trading: A Geometry of Pricing Measures
papers.abstract: How much model doubt can an investor bear before they stop trading? Our investor treats every model within a given Kullback-Leibler divergence of their reference model as plausible. In a finite one-period market, they hold no risky asset exactly when this doubt reaches the smallest divergence of a pricing measure from their model, for every smooth, strictly increasing, strictly concave utility; non-traded claims then have intervals of no-trade prices. Below this threshold, for log utility and in a given market, doubt acts exactly like higher constant relative risk aversion; their robust pricing measure moves from the log-utility measure toward the pricing measure at that smallest divergence. With a century of U.S. data, a log investor who doubts the Black-Scholes mean return over its 95% confidence interval acts like a fully trusting investor with relative risk aversion of about 1.8 instead of 1. Implied doubt turns a quote into a radius; the mean VIX implies doubt beyond the threshold, but whether significantly so depends on the reference model. By a known identity, real-world, pricing, and share (stock-numeraire) measures form a triangle whose Pythagorean defect is a log risk premium; one side is half the squared (ideal) VIX times the horizon. Since 1990, the U.S. defect averages about 10% per year, about 1 point of it entropy premium.

First-Principles Investigation of the {ScSe2} TMDs Monolayer: Structural Stability, Electronic and Optical Properties
Kinetic moment estimates and a one-sided Lyapunov barrier for the relativistic fermionic Michie-King equation
Symmetry classes of hyperdeterminant wavefunctions: Application to phase transitions between a bosonic fractional Chern insulator and superfluids
Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can transfer agile robot skills from simulation to the real world, but closing the sim-to-real gap by domain randomization requires expert physics knowledge, and simulator calibration from real data typically targets a few hand-picked parameters. Even then, simulators miss real-world effects, and environments reconstructed from onboard perception inherit sensing errors that limit policy improvement. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), which uses conditional flow matching to calibrate simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity domains online during deployment. Residual fidelity captures sim-to-real dynamics discrepancies and perception-induced environment uncertainty. NFC operates in a latent space so that realistic environments can be sampled from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning. The framework is informative: the pretrained policy is fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected, sequential NFC seeds its proposal from the simulation-pretrained estimator, and a hallucination policy modulates posterior uncertainty following optimism in the face of uncertainty. NFC attains the most accurate posteriors among established simulation-based inference methods on five robots with up to 39 physical parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain. On a wheeled robot with a broken wheel axle deployed on snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC raises success on rough terrain from 26% to 70% and reduces orientation jerk by 88%. Code and videos will be released upon publication.

papers.title: Associative operators and their iterated lifts: classification and cocycle identities
papers.abstract: The inverse problem of an inhomogeneous functional equation asks for which right-hand sides the equation is solvable. For the Cauchy equation and for the quadratic equation a necessary condition is a cocycle identity, and the two identities have a common form. We take this form as a definition. An operator from functions of one variable to functions of two variables can be lifted to functions of several variables, one argument at a time. We call it associative when its two iterated lifts from one variable to three coincide, that is, when every function in its image satisfies the corresponding cocycle identity. Composition with an associative binary operation is the model case. The Cauchy difference, the d'Alembert operator and the Jordan-von Neumann operator are associative as well. We prove that all iterated lifts of the same length of an associative operator coincide. Over abelian groups we classify, under suitable hypotheses, the associative integer combinations of translations, embeddings and the evaluation at the origin. For a composition operator the cocycle identity characterises the image over monoids and over bands. Over an arbitrary semigroup we reduce this question to the injectivity of a canonical map.

papers.title: Threshold Generalized Autoregressive Moving Average Models
papers.abstract: Non-Gaussian time series often exhibit nonlinear dynamics and changes in dependence structures that may not be adequately captured by conventional single-regime models. To address this limitation, we introduce a class of threshold generalized autoregressive moving-average (TGARMA) models that combines observation-driven GARMA dynamics with threshold-based regime switching. The proposed framework accommodates multiple regimes, determined by a lagged endogenous or exogenous threshold variable, and allows regression coefficients, autoregressive and moving-average orders and coefficients, and, where applicable, dispersion parameters to vary across regimes. Parameters are estimated by maximum partial likelihood, while model selection is conducted using information criteria. We examine model admissibility and stability, assess model adequacy through residual diagnostics, and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to investigate the finite-sample performance of the estimators.
